question:
The following sentence has an error in its tense. Identify the error and select the correct sentence from the options.
If you had apprised me about your problem earlier, I would have allow you to go.
option_1: If you had apprised me about your problem earlier, I would have allowed you to go.
option_2: If you apprised me about your problem earlier, I would have allowed you to go.
option_3: If you had apprised me about your problem earlier, I would allow you to go.
option_4: If you can apprise me about your problem earlier, I would have allowed you to go.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. If you had apprised me about your problem earlier, I would have allowed you to go.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is a Type 3 Conditional Sentence (used for an unreal/hypothetical situation in the past that did not actually happen).

• Rule — Third Conditional: If + Subject + had + V3, Subject + would/could/might + have + V3.
◦ The "if" clause takes "had + past participle", and the main clause takes "would have + past participle".

• In the given sentence, the "if" clause "If you had apprised me" is correctly in the had + V3 form, but the main clause wrongly uses "would have allow" (base form) instead of "would have allowed" (V3/past participle).

• Correcting the verb form gives: If you had apprised me about your problem earlier, I would have allowed you to go.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "If you apprised me... I would have allowed..." is incorrect because it mixes a Simple Past "if" clause with a Third Conditional main clause; both clauses must match the Type 3 pattern.

• Option 3: "If you had apprised me... I would allow..." is incorrect because the main clause uses "would + V1" (Type 2 pattern) instead of "would have + V3".

• Option 4: "If you can apprise me... I would have allowed..." is incorrect because "can apprise" (present ability) does not match the hypothetical past sense required by the sentence.

NOTE

• Third Conditional sentences describe imaginary results of imaginary past actions — situations that could have happened but did not.

• Do not confuse the three conditionals: Type 1 (If + V1, will + V1) for real/possible future events; Type 2 (If + V2, would + V1) for unreal present/future; Type 3 (If + had + V3, would have + V3) for unreal past.

question: Select the option with the correct use of article(s).
option_1: She kept lot of rules in her life, due to which she is flourishing today.
option_2: She kept an lot of rules in her life, due to which she is flourishing today.
option_3: She kept a lot of rules in her life, due to which she is flourishing today.
option_4: She kept the lot of rules in her life, due to which she is flourishing today.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. She kept a lot of rules in her life, due to which she is flourishing today.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "a lot of" is a fixed quantifying expression meaning "a large number/amount of", and it always takes the indefinite article "a", never "an" or "the", and it is never used without any article at all.

• Rule — Articles with fixed quantifiers: Expressions like "a lot of", "a few", "a little", "a couple of" always begin with "a" because they function as set phrases, regardless of whether the noun that follows is singular or plural.

• Applying the rule to the sentence, the correct quantifying phrase is "a lot of rules".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "kept lot of rules" is incorrect because the article "a" has been dropped altogether before the fixed phrase "lot of".

• Option 2: "kept an lot of rules" is incorrect because "an" is used only before words beginning with a vowel sound, and in any case the fixed phrase is always "a lot of", never "an lot of".

• Option 4: "kept the lot of rules" is incorrect because "the" (definite article) wrongly replaces the fixed indefinite phrase "a lot of", changing the intended general meaning to a specific one.

NOTE

• "A" is used before words beginning with a consonant sound (a rule, a university); "an" is used before words beginning with a vowel sound (an hour, an MBA).

• Other fixed quantifier phrases that always take "a": "a great deal of", "a number of", "a good many of".

question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.
The project was completed / more quicker / than expected.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. more quicker.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the phrase "more quicker", which is a case of double comparative — using two comparative markers together for the same adjective.

• Rule — Degrees of Comparison: A comparative degree is formed either by adding "-er" to a short adjective (quick → quicker) or by placing "more" before a longer adjective (more beautiful), but never both together.

• Since "quicker" is already the comparative form of "quick", adding "more" before it is grammatically redundant and incorrect; the correct phrase is simply "quicker".

• Corrected sentence: The project was completed quicker than expected.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because the sentence does contain a clear grammatical error in the comparative form.

• Option 3: "The project was completed" is incorrect because this part of the sentence is grammatically correct as it stands (simple past passive).

• Option 4: "than expected" is incorrect because this part is a correctly formed comparative clause and contains no error.

NOTE

• Common double-comparative errors to watch for in SSC exams: "more better" (→ better), "more easier" (→ easier), "most best" (→ best/the best), "more nicer" (→ nicer).

• Similarly, avoid double superlatives such as "most best" — use either "most beautiful" or "the best", never combine "most" with an "-est" form.

question:
There is an error in the given sentence. From the options given, identify the sentence that corrects the error to make it a grammatically accurate sentence.
Harmit is not innocent such as Uday.
option_1: Harmit is not as innocent more than Uday.
option_2: Harmit is not as much as innocent as Uday.
option_3: Harmit is not as innocent as Uday.
option_4: Harmit is not innocent than Uday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Harmit is not as innocent as Uday.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence uses "such as" to make a comparison of equality, which is grammatically wrong; "such as" is used to introduce examples, not to compare two things.

• Rule — Comparison of Equality: To compare two things as being equal in some quality, the structure "as + adjective + as" is used: Subject + is/are + as + adjective + as + object.

• For a negative comparison of equality, the structure is "not as + adjective + as", e.g., "Harmit is not as innocent as Uday", meaning Uday is more innocent than Harmit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "not as innocent more than Uday" is incorrect because it wrongly mixes the "as...as" structure with "more than", which belongs to the comparative degree, not comparison of equality.

• Option 2: "not as much as innocent as Uday" is incorrect because it inserts the redundant phrase "as much as" before the adjective, breaking the standard "as + adjective + as" pattern.

• Option 4: "not innocent than Uday" is incorrect because "than" is used only with the comparative degree (e.g., "more innocent than"), and here the base adjective "innocent" is used without "more", making the sentence ungrammatical.

NOTE

• "Such as" is correctly used to give examples, e.g., "Fruits such as apples and mangoes are healthy."

• Do not confuse comparison of equality (as...as) with the comparative degree (more...than / adjective+er...than) — they follow entirely different structures.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Many parents think of overweight children as ‘cute’ and cuddly. However, obesity must not be (1) ________ as a healthy sign. (2) ________ obese children grow up, they will be more prone (3) ________ health problems like high blood pressure (4) ________ diabetes. Today, overweight children are becoming a common (5) ________ in many countries.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. seen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: **"obesity must not be ________ as a healthy sign", which requires a passive voice construction** after the modal verb "must".

• Rule — Passive Voice with Modals: Modal + be + V3 (past participle), e.g., must be done, should be seen, may be taken.

• Since the auxiliary "be" is already present, the blank must be filled with the past participle (V3) of "see", which is "seen".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "saw" is incorrect because "saw" is the simple past form (V2), which cannot follow "must not be".

• Option 3: "see" is incorrect because it is the base form (V1); the passive structure after "be" always requires the past participle.

• Option 4: "seeing" is incorrect because the present participle (V-ing) does not fit the passive "modal + be + V3" pattern.

NOTE

• The three forms of "see" are: see (V1) – saw (V2) – seen (V3); only "seen" can be used after any form of "be" in the passive voice.

• Common SSC modal + passive constructions: must be done, should be completed, can be solved, may be taken.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Many parents think of overweight children as ‘cute’ and cuddly. However, obesity must not be (1) ________ as a healthy sign. (2) ________ obese children grow up, they will be more prone (3) ________ health problems like high blood pressure (4) ________ diabetes. Today, overweight children are becoming a common (5) ________ in many countries.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. When.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank connects two clauses: **"________ obese children grow up, they will be more prone to health problems..." — the sentence needs a connector that shows a time relationship** between "growing up" and "becoming prone to health problems".

• Rule — Subordinating Conjunctions of Time: Words like "when", "as", "while" are used to join a time clause to a main clause, e.g., "When he grows up, he will understand."

• Here, "When" correctly introduces the time clause showing that the health problems arise as a result of/at the time of the children growing up.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Who" is incorrect because "who" is a relative pronoun used for persons within a single clause, not a conjunction joining two clauses.

• Option 3: "What" is incorrect because "what" is an interrogative/relative pronoun referring to a thing, and does not fit the time-clause structure here.

• Option 4: "Where" is incorrect because "where" is used to indicate place, not time, and the sentence is concerned with a time-based/causal sequence, not a location.

NOTE

• Common conjunctions of time tested in SSC cloze passages: when, while, as, before, after, until, as soon as.

• Do not confuse conjunctions (when, where used to join clauses) with plain question words used in direct questions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Many parents think of overweight children as ‘cute’ and cuddly. However, obesity must not be (1) ________ as a healthy sign. (2) ________ obese children grow up, they will be more prone (3) ________ health problems like high blood pressure (4) ________ diabetes. Today, overweight children are becoming a common (5) ________ in many countries.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. to.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank appears in the phrase **"more prone ________ health problems", which tests the correct preposition collocation** with the adjective "prone".

• Rule — Fixed Preposition: The adjective "prone" is always followed by the preposition "to" — "prone to something" means "likely to suffer from or be affected by something".

• Therefore, the correct phrase is "more prone to health problems".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "in" is incorrect because "prone" never collocates with "in"; it does not fit the fixed phrase.

• Option 3: "at" is incorrect because "at" is not the preposition that follows "prone" in standard English usage.

• Option 4: "on" is incorrect because "on" is not used with "prone"; the only correct preposition is "to".

NOTE

• Other adjectives that take the fixed preposition "to": liable to, subject to, addicted to, accustomed to, prior to.

• Do not confuse "prone to" with "proud of" or "keen on", which take different prepositions.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Many parents think of overweight children as ‘cute’ and cuddly. However, obesity must not be (1) ________ as a healthy sign. (2) ________ obese children grow up, they will be more prone (3) ________ health problems like high blood pressure (4) ________ diabetes. Today, overweight children are becoming a common (5) ________ in many countries.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. or.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank joins two related health problems: **"high blood pressure ________ diabetes"**, both being examples of the "health problems" mentioned earlier — the connector must simply link two related items in a list.

• Rule — Use of "or": "Or" is a coordinating conjunction used to connect words or phrases that present alternatives or additional related items in a list, e.g., "tea or coffee", "high blood pressure or diabetes".

• Since "neither" and "nor" must be used together as a correlative pair (neither...nor), and "never" is an adverb of frequency (not a conjunction), only "or" correctly fits as a simple connector here.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "neither" is incorrect because "neither" must be paired with "nor" (neither...nor...) and cannot stand alone as a simple connector.

• Option 3: "nor" is incorrect for the same reason — "nor" is used only after "neither" (or a negative clause) as part of a correlative pair, which is absent here.

• Option 4: "never" is incorrect because it is an adverb meaning "at no time", and cannot function as a conjunction linking two nouns.

NOTE

• Correlative conjunctions commonly tested by SSC: either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also, both...and.

• "Or" is used for alternatives/lists, while "and" is used for simple addition — both are simple coordinating conjunctions, unlike the correlative pairs above.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Many parents think of overweight children as ‘cute’ and cuddly. However, obesity must not be (1) ________ as a healthy sign. (2) ________ obese children grow up, they will be more prone (3) ________ health problems like high blood pressure (4) ________ diabetes. Today, overweight children are becoming a common (5) ________ in many countries.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. sight.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the phrase **"overweight children are becoming a common ________ in many countries"**, which requires a word that collocates with "common" to mean "something frequently seen/observed".

• Rule — Fixed Collocation: The phrase "a common sight" is a set expression meaning "something that is often seen and is therefore not unusual".

• Applying this, the sentence correctly reads: "overweight children are becoming a common sight in many countries."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "might" is incorrect because "might" is a modal verb and does not fit as a noun after "a common".

• Option 3: "light" is incorrect because "a common light" is not a meaningful or standard collocation in this context.

• Option 4: "tight" is incorrect because "tight" is an adjective and cannot function as the noun required after "a common" in this sentence.

NOTE

• Other fixed noun collocations with "common": common sense, common ground, common knowledge, common courtesy.

• Words that sound similar but differ in meaning: sight (vision/something seen), site (location), cite (to quote) — a frequently tested homophone set in SSC exams.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Riding a horse was a piece of cake for him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. a very easy task.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a piece of cake" means something that is very easy to do or achieve, requiring little effort. (बहुत आसान काम)
◦ Example: The math test was a piece of cake for her; she finished it in ten minutes.

• In the given sentence, "Riding a horse was a piece of cake for him" means that riding a horse was a very easy task for him.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: An everyday affair (रोज़मर्रा की बात): Something that happens routinely every day — this refers to frequency, not ease, so it does not match the meaning of the idiom.

• Option 3: Confusing work (उलझन भरा काम): Something puzzling or hard to understand — this is nearly opposite to the intended meaning.

• Option 4: A very difficult task (बहुत कठिन काम): This is the direct opposite of "a piece of cake", which specifically means something easy, not difficult.

NOTE

• Other idioms meaning "very easy" often asked in SSC: "a walk in the park", "child's play", "as easy as ABC", "a cakewalk".

• Do not confuse "a piece of cake" (easy task) with "to have one's cake and eat it too" (to want two incompatible things).

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Blowing smoke
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To lie to perplex others.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "blowing smoke" means to say things that are not true, or to exaggerate/mislead, in order to confuse, impress or deceive someone. (दूसरों को भ्रमित करने के लिए झूठ बोलना)
◦ Example: Don't believe his promises — he's just blowing smoke to win votes.

• The expression comes from the idea of creating a "smokescreen" — using empty or misleading words to obscure the truth, just as smoke obscures vision.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To tease someone relentlessly (लगातार चिढ़ाना): This describes persistent mockery, which is unrelated to the idea of deception through false talk.

• Option 2: To hide something (कुछ छिपाना): While smoke can obscure things literally, the idiom specifically refers to deceptive talk, not physically hiding an object.

• Option 3: To burn something important (महत्वपूर्ण चीज़ जलाना): This is a literal interpretation of "smoke" and does not reflect the idiomatic meaning at all.

NOTE

• Related idioms of deception commonly tested in SSC: "to pull the wool over someone's eyes" (to deceive), "to beat around the bush" (to avoid the main point), "to smell a rat" (to suspect deception).

• "Smoke and mirrors" is a closely related idiom meaning a deceptive or misleading explanation.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
It is no exaggeration to say the Hussain Sagar Lake is an integral element of Hyderabad and Hyderabad's history.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. extra.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "integral" means essential or necessary for completeness; forming a fundamental/basic part of something. (अनिवार्य/अभिन्न)

• Its antonym must convey the opposite idea — something that is not essential, additional, or dispensable. The word "extra" means additional or more than what is necessary, which is the correct opposite of "integral". (अतिरिक्त/गैर-ज़रूरी)

• In the sentence, while the lake is described as an "integral" (essential) part of the city, its antonym "extra" would describe something merely additional, not essential.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Essential (अनिवार्य): This is a synonym of "integral", not its opposite — both words describe something necessary/fundamental.

• Option 2: Total (कुल): This means "complete" or "entire in amount", which does not express the opposite of "integral".

• Option 4: Inherent (अंतर्निहित): This means "existing as a natural or permanent part of something", which is again close in meaning to "integral", not opposite to it.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "integral": fundamental, intrinsic, indispensable, vital, essential.

• Other antonyms of "integral" that may appear in SSC: peripheral, unnecessary, dispensable, optional.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
His opponents viewed him as stubborn, dogmatic, and inflexible.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Amenable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "dogmatic" means stubbornly asserting one's opinions as true without allowing for debate or contradiction; rigidly inflexible in one's views. (हठधर्मी/अड़ियल)

• Its antonym must express the opposite quality — being open to persuasion, suggestion, or advice. "Amenable" means willing to be influenced, guided, or persuaded; responsive to suggestions, which is the correct opposite of "dogmatic". (सहमत होने योग्य/लचीला)

• In the sentence, a person described as "dogmatic" would refuse to change his views, whereas an "amenable" person would readily accept advice or persuasion.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Dishonest (बेईमान): This means "not truthful", which relates to honesty, not to rigidity of opinion — it is not the opposite of "dogmatic".

• Option 2: Biased (पक्षपाती): This means "having an unfair preference", which is a related but distinct trait from being dogmatic, and is not its antonym.

• Option 3: Careless (लापरवाह): This means "lacking attention or caution", which has no direct opposite relationship with "dogmatic".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "dogmatic": opinionated, obstinate, rigid, inflexible, arbitrary.

• Other antonyms of "dogmatic" useful for SSC: flexible, open-minded, receptive, accommodating.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Dissappoint.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Disappoint" — to fail to fulfil the hopes or expectations of someone.
◦ Example: His poor performance in the exam did not disappoint his teachers, who had expected it.

• Spelling key: DIS + APPOINT. The prefix "dis-" contributes only one "s", while the root word "appoint" already contains a double "pp"; the given word "Dissappoint" wrongly doubles the "s" instead, making it incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Foresee" — this is spelt correctly; it means "to be aware of beforehand".

• Option 2: "Rebuke" — this is spelt correctly; it means "to express sharp disapproval".

• Option 3: "Seize" — this is spelt correctly; it means "to take hold of suddenly and forcibly" (remember: it is an exception to the "i before e except after c" rule).

NOTE

• Words with the "dis-" prefix keep only a single "s" from the prefix but often double the first consonant of the root, e.g., disappear, disappoint, disapprove (single "s", double "p").

• The common SSC trap is writing "diss-" where only one "s" is required — always check: disappoint (correct) vs. "dissappoint" (incorrect).

question:
Select the option that will most suitably substitute the underlined part of the given sentence.
He was not happy until he gave up his job and live as a fakir in the forests.
option_1: unless he gave up his job and lives
option_2: until he gave up his job and lived
option_3: until he gave up his job and lives
option_4: until he gives up his job and lived
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. until he gave up his job and lived.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence contains two verbs joined by "and" — "gave up" and "live" — describing actions that happened together in the past; both verbs must be in the same tense for grammatical parallelism.

• Rule — Parallel Structure: When two or more verbs are joined by a coordinating conjunction (and/or/but) and refer to the same subject and time frame, all the verbs must be in the same tense form.

• Since "gave up" is in the simple past tense, the second verb must also be in the simple past — "lived", not "live". Corrected: "until he gave up his job and lived as a fakir in the forests."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "unless he gave up his job and lives" is incorrect because "unless" (meaning "if not") changes the intended meaning, and "lives" also breaks tense parallelism with "gave up".

• Option 3: "until he gave up his job and lives" is incorrect because "lives" (present tense) does not agree with the past tense verb "gave up".

• Option 4: "until he gives up his job and lived" is incorrect because "gives up" (present tense) does not agree with the past tense verb "lived"; the tenses are again mismatched.

NOTE

• Always check sentences with two or more verbs joined by "and" for tense parallelism — a very common SSC error type.

• Do not confuse "until" (up to the time that/till) with "unless" (if...not) — they have different meanings and are not interchangeable.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the word 'bold' in the given sentence.
A person can be friendly, timid, clever, or fearless based on the context of the situation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. timid.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "bold" means having or showing courage and confidence; not afraid to take risks. (साहसी/निड़र)

• Its antonym must express the opposite quality — a lack of courage or confidence. "Timid" means showing a lack of courage or confidence; easily frightened, making it the correct opposite of "bold". (डरपोक/भीरु)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Friendly (मित्रवत्): This means "kind and pleasant towards others", which relates to sociability, not courage — it is not the opposite of "bold".

• Option 2: Clever (चतुर): This means "quick to understand and learn", which relates to intelligence, not courage, and is unrelated to "bold" as an antonym pair.

• Option 4: Fearless (निड़र): This is a synonym of "bold" (both mean courageous/unafraid), not its opposite.

NOTE

• Synonyms of "bold": brave, courageous, daring, fearless, valiant.

• Other antonyms of "bold" useful for SSC: cowardly, shy, meek, diffident, cautious.

question:
Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the given sentence.
'Vande Mataram', a poignant poem, is obviously and indisputebly the premier national song of India.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Indisputebly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Indisputably" — in a way that cannot be questioned or denied; unquestionably.
◦ Example: The evidence indisputably proved his innocence.

• Spelling key: The word is built as IN + DIS + PUTE + ABLY, following the pattern of the adjective "indisputable" (which ends in -able, not "-eble"); the adverb is formed by changing "-able" to "-ably". The given word "Indisputebly" wrongly uses "e" in place of "a".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Obviously" — this is spelt correctly; it means "in a way that is easily perceived or understood; clearly".

• Option 2: "Premier" — this is spelt correctly; it means "first in importance, order, or position; foremost".

• Option 4: "Poignant" — this is spelt correctly; it means "evoking a keen sense of sadness or regret".

NOTE

• Words ending in "-able/-ably" vs "-ible/-ibly" are a common SSC trap: indisputable, comfortable, reasonable (–able) versus possible, responsible, visible (–ible) — there is no fixed rule, so such words must be learnt individually.

• Related words: dispute (verb/noun), disputable (adjective), indisputable (adjective), indisputably (adverb).

question:
Select the most appropriate homonyms from the given alternatives to fill in the blanks.
He ________ imitate the playful movement of the ________.
Alternatives:
A. does (female deer)
B. does
C. dose
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. B, A.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence has two blanks: **"He ________ imitate the playful movement of the ________."**

• The first blank needs the auxiliary verb "does" (used for emphasis before a base verb — "does imitate"), which corresponds to alternative B (does).

• The second blank needs a noun meaning female deer, which corresponds to alternative A (does — female deer), since the plural of "doe" (a female deer) is "does". The completed sentence reads: "He does imitate the playful movement of the does."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 (B, A).

Additional Information

• Option 1: "C, B" (dose, does) is incorrect because "dose" (a measured quantity of medicine) does not fit the auxiliary-verb slot in the first blank.

• Option 3: "A, B" (does-female deer, does) is incorrect because it reverses the correct order — the auxiliary verb "does" must come first, and the noun "does" (female deer) must come second.

• Option 4: "A, C" (does-female deer, dose) is incorrect because neither word fits its respective blank correctly — the auxiliary verb is missing from the first blank, and "dose" (medicine) makes no sense as "the playful movement of the dose".

NOTE

• Homonyms/homophones are words that sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning — e.g., does (verb) / doe's / dose, there/their/they're, witch/which.

• "Doe" refers to a female deer (or rabbit/hare); its plural is "does", which is pronounced the same as the auxiliary verb "does" — a frequently tested homophone pair in SSC exams.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Dhruv's anger blazed of uncontrollably.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. anger blazed up.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrasal verb "blaze up" means to burst into sudden and intense activity or emotion; to flare up suddenly, and is the standard collocation used with emotions like anger.

• Rule — Phrasal Verb Collocation: Certain verbs combine with fixed particles to form phrasal verbs with a specific idiomatic meaning; "blaze" correctly combines with "up" (not "of", "onwards", "after" or "into") when describing a sudden intensification of emotion.

• Corrected sentence: "Dhruv's anger blazed up uncontrollably."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "anger blazed onwards" is incorrect because "blaze onwards" is not a recognised English collocation/phrasal verb.

• Option 2: "anger blazed after" is incorrect because "blaze after" is not a standard phrasal verb combination with "anger".

• Option 4: "anger blazed into" is incorrect because "blaze into" is not the correct fixed particle used with sudden emotional outbursts; it does not form a recognised idiomatic phrase here.

NOTE

• Other phrasal verbs describing sudden emotion: "flare up" (sudden anger), "boil over" (anger reaching a peak), "erupt" (sudden intense emotion).

• "Blaze" also combines with other particles in different senses, e.g., "blaze a trail" (to be the first to do something new).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.
The company do not broke the law at any time.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. does not break.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject "The company" is a singular noun, and the sentence is in the Simple Present Tense (indicated by "at any time", describing a general/habitual fact).

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement in Simple Present: A singular subject (he/she/it or a singular noun) takes "does" + base form (V1) in the negative, i.e., does not + V1, e.g., "does not break", "does not go".

• Applying the rule, the sentence must read: "The company does not break the law at any time."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "do not brakes" is incorrect because "do" does not agree with the singular subject "the company" (should be "does"), and "brakes" incorrectly adds "-s" to the verb after a negative auxiliary.

• Option 2: "did not breaking" is incorrect because after the auxiliary "did", the verb must be in the base form, not the "-ing" form.

• Option 3: "did not broken" is incorrect because after "did", the verb must be in the base form ("break"), not the past participle "broken"; also, "did" would incorrectly shift the sentence to the past tense.

NOTE

• Singular collective nouns like "company", "team", "family", "government" normally take a singular verb in standard SSC usage.

• Remember the auxiliary pattern: Simple Present negative → does/do + not + V1; Simple Past negative → did + not + V1 (the base form never changes after "did").

question:
Select the most appropriate homonym to fill in the blank.
Sonu eats ________ like a rabbit.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. carrot.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence requires a word for a vegetable that rabbits are famously known to eat, which is "carrot" — a long, orange root vegetable.

• The words "karat", "carrot", "carat" and "caret" are all homophones (they sound alike) but differ completely in meaning and spelling; only the meaning of the sentence can determine the correct one.

• Since the sentence is about eating like a rabbit, the contextually correct word is "carrot": "Sonu eats carrot like a rabbit."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "karat" is incorrect because "karat" is a unit measuring the purity of gold, which does not fit the context of eating.

• Option 3: "carat" is incorrect because "carat" is a unit of weight used for gemstones (like diamonds), unrelated to food.

• Option 4: "caret" is incorrect because a "caret" is a proofreading/typographical mark (^) used to indicate an insertion in text, which has no connection to eating.

NOTE

• The homophone set karat/carat/caret/carrot is frequently tested in SSC exams — remember: karat = gold purity, carat = gemstone weight, caret = insertion mark (^), carrot = vegetable.

• Always determine the correct homophone using the context/meaning of the sentence, since all sound identical when spoken.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can best replace the bracketed word to fill in the blank
His ________ stature was not a measure of his overall personality. (scrawny)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. thin.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The bracketed word "scrawny" means unattractively thin and bony; very lean. (दुबला-पतला)
◦ Example: The scrawny stray dog looked as though it hadn't eaten in days.

• Among the given options, "thin" is the closest and most appropriate word to convey the sense of "scrawny" — someone of slight, lean build. (पतला)

• Completed sentence: "His thin stature was not a measure of his overall personality."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Muscular (मांसल): This means "having well-developed muscles", which is nearly the opposite of "scrawny" (which suggests a lack of muscle/flesh).

• Option 3: Keen (उत्सुक/तीक्ष्ण): This means "eager" or "sharp", and has no relation to physical build, so it cannot substitute "scrawny".

• Option 4: Sickly (बीमार जैसा): This means "often ill or in poor health", which describes health rather than physical leanness, making it a less precise fit than "thin".

NOTE

• Words meaning "thin": lean, lanky, skinny, gaunt, slender, scrawny.

• Words meaning "fat/well-built": stout, sturdy, muscular, burly, plump.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined word in the given sentence.
The family was saved from the burning building by the brave firefighter.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. fearless.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "brave" means showing courage; ready to face and endure danger or pain without showing fear. (बहादुर/साहसी)
◦ Example: The brave firefighter rushed into the burning building to rescue the trapped family.

• "Fearless" means without fear; showing no fear in the face of danger, which closely matches the meaning of "brave" and is the most suitable substitute. (निड़र)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Unafraid (निर्भय): While close in meaning, "unafraid" simply means "not feeling fear"; "fearless" is the more precise and standard synonym of "brave" tested here.

• Option 3: Timid (डरपोक): This means "easily frightened; lacking courage", which is the opposite of "brave".

• Option 4: Cowardly (कायर): This means "lacking courage; showing fear", which is also directly opposite to the meaning of "brave".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "brave": courageous, valiant, bold, daring, gallant, intrepid.

• Antonyms of "brave": cowardly, timid, fearful, cautious, meek.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Respect
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Honour.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Respect" means a feeling of deep admiration for someone or something elicited by their abilities, qualities, or achievements; esteem. (सम्मान/आदर)

• "Honour" means high respect or esteem; regard felt or shown for someone, which closely matches the meaning of "Respect" and is therefore its correct synonym. (सम्मान/इज़्ज़त)
◦ Example: Students should honour and respect their teachers.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Disrespect (अनादर): This means "a lack of respect; discourtesy", which is the direct antonym of "Respect", not its synonym.

• Option 3: Attend (उपस्थित होना): This means "to be present at an event" or "to deal with something", which has no meaning connection to "Respect".

• Option 4: Invalidate (अमान्य करना): This means "to make something legally or factually void/invalid", which is entirely unrelated in meaning to "Respect".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "Respect": esteem, regard, reverence, admiration, deference.

• Antonyms of "Respect": disrespect, contempt, scorn, disdain.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Shame
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Pride.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Shame" means a painful feeling of humiliation or distress caused by the consciousness of wrong or foolish behaviour. (शर्म/लज्जा)

• "Pride" means a feeling of deep pleasure or satisfaction derived from one's own achievements or qualities; a sense of self-respect and dignity, which is the correct opposite of "Shame". (गर्व/अभिमान)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Disgrace (अपमान): This means "loss of reputation or respect; shame", which is a synonym of "Shame", not its antonym.

• Option 2: Defamation (मानहानि): This means "the act of damaging someone's good reputation", which is closely related in meaning to disgrace/shame, not opposite to it.

• Option 4: Fear (डर): This means "an unpleasant emotion caused by the belief that someone/something is dangerous", which is a different emotion altogether and not the antonym of "Shame".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "Shame": disgrace, humiliation, embarrassment, ignominy, dishonour.

• Other antonyms of "Shame" useful for SSC: honour, dignity, glory, self-respect.
